I’ve left the Microsoft Debugger Platform team twice, and each time I’ve started writing my own debugger. I must really like debuggers or something. This time, I have two reasons for writing a new debugger. The first is because I want to learn Rust better, and writing something I already understand pretty well seems like a good way to learn. The second reason is to make it easier for people to learn how a debugger works. Using Rust also helps here because there are lots of crates that can take care of things like symbols and disassembly, and it will let us focus on the core ideas involved in writing a debugger.

I’m a Rust novice, and if you’re looking to learn Rust better, I’d suggest to start with https://www.rust-lang.org/learn. I’m not going to try to explain too much about the Rust code, but the main concepts and APIs will apply across language. You should be able to follow along even without much knowledge of Rust. Those of you who read this and know Rust better than me, please feel free to create issues in the GitHub repo. Or even better, make a pull request! The code for this first part is in a branch called “part1”, and you can see the full code here. If you want to follow along, I suggest cloning the whole repo locally and viewing it in a good IDE like VS Code with the rust-analyzer plugin.

What is a debugger?

First, what is a debugger? There are lots of tools that are “debugging tools” but when most people hear “debugger” they usually think of a tool that can analyze either a running system or a static snapshot (such as a core file, crash dump, or VM snapshot)1. Most debuggers like GDB, LLDB, Visual Studio, and WinDbg can do both of these things. We’ll start by creating a debugger that supports live usermode debugging on Windows. The core concepts will apply to nearly any OS, with the main differences being the OS APIs for debugging a process and the terminology that is used for certain concepts.

In Windows, there are just a few APIs that provide the necessary functionality for implementing a debugger. Most of these are described on MSDN in the Debugging Functions page. Note that these are the APIs that are used by a debugger such as Visual Studio or WinDbg. The core engine of WinDbg is called DbgEng, and has its own set of APIs that can be accessed through the IDebugClient interface and related APIs. These higher level APIs and are very powerful, with built in stack unwinding, symbol analysis, flow control, disassembly, scripting, and lots of other capabilities. If you want to automate some debugging task, this is a better API to use. But that’s not what we’re going to do in this post series. We are going to implement a debugger from scratch using the most basic APIs provided by the OS.

There are a number of other functions we’ll need to interact with a running process, but these APIs are not debugging-specific. We’ll cover those as we encounter them.

Basic structure

At the center of a live debugging session is an event loop. A debugger registers for debug events from a target process by “attaching” to it. For each event that occurs, the OS will freeze the target process and notify the debugger with information about that debug event. The debugger then has the opportunity to examine or manipulate the state of the target process. The debugger then continues from the debug event.

There’s a ton of complexity embedded in here, but most of that complexity is in examining and manipulating the state of the target process. We’ll start by creating a debugger that attaches to a process, monitors the debug events, and continues from them to allow the process to execute normally. That part is relatively straightforward, and will give us a basis for other functionality that can be built on top of this.

On Windows, there are two main ways to attach to a process. If there is already a process running that we want to attach to, we can use the DebugActiveProcess API, which takes a single parameter with the process ID that we want to debug.2. There is no handle or any other information passed back as a result of this API call. Instead, an implicit connection is created between the target process and the debugger process. To stop debugging a process, you call DebugActiveProcessStop, which also takes a single parameter of a process ID.

The second way to attach to a process is by creating the process in an attached state. To do that, we use the same CreateProcessW function that you would normally use to debug a process and include the DEBUG_ONLY_THIS_PROCESS or DEBUG_PROCESS flag as part of the dwCreationFlags parameter (documented as part of the Process Creation Flags). The difference between these flags is whether you want to debug only the specific process you launched or if you want to debug that process and all of its child processes.

We’ll use CreateProcessW to start debugging a process:

105    let mut si: STARTUPINFOEXW = unsafe { std::mem::zeroed() };
106    si.StartupInfo.cb = std::mem::size_of::<STARTUPINFOEXW>() as u32;
107    let mut pi: PROCESS_INFORMATION = unsafe { std::mem::zeroed() };
108    let ret = unsafe {
109        CreateProcessW(
110            null(),                                       // lpApplicationName
111            command_line_buffer.as_mut_ptr(),             // lpCommandLine
112            null(),                                       // lpProcessAttributes
113            null(),                                       // lpThreadAttributes
114            FALSE,                                        // bInheritHandles
115            DEBUG_ONLY_THIS_PROCESS | CREATE_NEW_CONSOLE, // dwCreationFlags
116            null(),                                       // lpEnvironment
117            null(),                                       // lpCurrentDirectory
118            &mut si.StartupInfo,                          // lpStartupInfo
119            &mut pi,                                      // lpProcessInformation
120        )
121    };

There are a lot of parameters to CreateProcessW, but we can ignore the optional parameters to start. Later, we may want to give a user of this debugger the ability to customize certain aspects, but for now we’ll simply use the entire command line passed in as the lpCommandLine. If you want to see how we got the command line to launch, see parse_command_line in the github repo for this project. We’ll also pass DEBUG_ONLY_THIS_PROCESS flag as part of dwCreationFlags. I’ve also specified CREATE_NEW_CONSOLE so that we won’t share a console when we debug a console app (CDB/NTSD will share a console with the target and I always found that confusing, and rarely useful). Finally, we’ll receive some important information as part of the lpProcessInformation parameter, which is an output parameter.

When CreateProcessW returns, the process will be initially suspended. No code will execute until the debugger process starts handling the debug events. So that’s what we’ll do next.

Monitoring debug events

Two functions are used to drive the event loop for a debugger in Windows. The first is the WaitForDebugEventEx function3. The second function is ContinueDebugEvent, which will resume the target process after handling the event. We will call these functions from main_debugger_loop.

56    loop {
57        let mut debug_event: DEBUG_EVENT = unsafe { std::mem::zeroed() };
58        unsafe {
59            WaitForDebugEventEx(&mut debug_event, INFINITE);
60        }

main.rs line 56

Something interesting you might note here is that the WaitForDebugEventEx function does not take in any process identifier. If a process is attached to multiple target processes, any call into WaitForDebugEventEx will monitor events for all attached processes4. The INFINITE parameter means that we will wait forever until a debug event is received. The event is described as a DEBUG_EVENT structure, which has fields for the thread ID, process ID, and an event code. Each event type has its own data structure, and the structures are stored as a union. You use the event code to determine which structure in the union is valid.

typedef struct _DEBUG_EVENT {
  DWORD dwDebugEventCode;
  DWORD dwProcessId;
  DWORD dwThreadId;
  union {
    EXCEPTION_DEBUG_INFO      Exception;
    CREATE_THREAD_DEBUG_INFO  CreateThread;
    CREATE_PROCESS_DEBUG_INFO CreateProcessInfo;
    EXIT_THREAD_DEBUG_INFO    ExitThread;
    EXIT_PROCESS_DEBUG_INFO   ExitProcess;
    LOAD_DLL_DEBUG_INFO       LoadDll;
    UNLOAD_DLL_DEBUG_INFO     UnloadDll;
    OUTPUT_DEBUG_STRING_INFO  DebugString;
    RIP_INFO                  RipInfo;
  } u;
} DEBUG_EVENT, *LPDEBUG_EVENT;

We’ll dig into that data in a later post. For now, we can just output which event we received.

66            EXIT_THREAD_DEBUG_EVENT => println!("ExitThread"),
67            EXIT_PROCESS_DEBUG_EVENT => println!("ExitProcess"),
68            LOAD_DLL_DEBUG_EVENT => println!("LoadDll"),
69            UNLOAD_DLL_DEBUG_EVENT => println!("UnloadDll"),
70            OUTPUT_DEBUG_STRING_EVENT => println!("OutputDebugString"),
71            RIP_EVENT => println!("RipEvent"),
72            _ => panic!("Unexpected debug event"),
73        }

We will loop forever handling debug events, but if we get an EXIT_PROCESS_DEBUG_EVENT, we can just exit the loop because we are only debugging a single process.

75        if debug_event.dwDebugEventCode == EXIT_PROCESS_DEBUG_EVENT {
76            break;
77        }

main.rs line 75

When we are done handling the event, we’ll call ContinueDebugEvent, which will allow the target process to resume execution. This function takes three parameters: a process ID, a thread ID, and a “continue status”. The first two are straightforward, and we can just use the process ID and thread ID that were fields of the DEBUG_EVENT. The continue status is a bit less obvious. It can be used to suppress the normal exception handling behavior by passing DBG_EXCEPTION_HANDLED. For now, we won’t worry about that and just always pass in DBG_EXCEPTION_NOT_HANDLED

79        unsafe {
80            ContinueDebugEvent(
81                debug_event.dwProcessId,
82                debug_event.dwThreadId,
83                DBG_EXCEPTION_NOT_HANDLED,
84            );
85        }

Putting it together

Build the project using cargo build, and then run it as dbgrs cmd and you’ll see some output in the current window, as well as seeing a new command window open up. If you close that window, you’ll see a few more lines of output, ending with an ExitProcess. For me, it looked like this:

D:\git\dbgrs\target\debug>dbgrs.exe cmd
Command line was: 'cmd'
CreateProcess
LoadDll
LoadDll
LoadDll
LoadDll
CreateThread
LoadDll
LoadDll
LoadDll
CreateThread
Exception
LoadDll
LoadDll
LoadDll
LoadDll
UnloadDll
UnloadDll
UnloadDll
ExitThread
ExitThread
ExitProcess

Each of those lines represents a single event returned from WaitForDebugEventEx. Each of these events is also an opportunity for a debugger to examine the state of the process. We haven’t yet started to look at the specific information from each event (like the name of the DLL that is loaded), but you can see how WinDbg would implement a command like sxe ld where the debugger can “break in” as soon as a module is loaded. All it means to “break in” when live debugging a process is simply wait before calling ContinueDebugEvent. After one of these events is returned, we could allow an interactive user to run some commands to examine the state of a process. When they were done and executed a command like g to continue execution, the debugger will call ContinueDebugEvent and then WaitForDebugEventEx again to wait for the next event.

Most of these events look pretty reasonable. We’d expect that a bunch of DLLs get loaded, a few threads get created, and eventually we unload some DLLs and exit the threads and process. There is one event hiding in the middle there, and it’s an Exception. That’s the initial breakpoint from ntdll!LdrpDoDebuggerBreak! As part of process startup, ntdll will trigger a breakpoint exception with an explicit int 3 on x865.

How we handle exception events will be one of the most important parts of debugging a live process. Everything from breakpoints, stepping, and application crashes are managed through the exception event. We’ll need to spend some time making sure we handle that correctly, so I will leave that for the next post. Until then, let me know what you thought of this on Twitter or Mastodon!

Footnotes

1 Many debuggers also integrate with some form of “time travel debugging” where a trace of execution is captured at various levels of granularity. While many of the concepts we talk about here also apply to time travel debugging, I’m going to skip talking about that here for the sake of brevity.

2 Using this API will check if the calling process actually has enough privilege to attach to the requested process. You cannot typically attach to an elevated process or process running for another user from an unelevated process. There are also certain processes that even an elevated administrator process can’t directly attach to. The documentation describes this as “it must be able to open the process for PROCESS_ALL_ACCESS.

3 There is a WaitForDebugEvent function (without the “Ex”), but this function will not correctly recieve Unicode strings that are generated from OutputDebugStringW. We want Unicode strings, so we’ll use the “Ex” version.

4 This means that it’s impossible for two separate modules to debug two separate targets from a single process. These are very old APIs that rely on process-wide state, and can NEVER be used by a module that expects to be loaded into an arbitrary process. Luckily this is rarely a problem in practice.

5 This breakpoint is only triggered if the process is being debugged. This is detected by checking the “BeingDebugged” flag of the PEB. If you break into the process prior to the initial breakpoint and set that flag to “0”, the initial breakpoint will be skipped.

blocks.html_en: First, what is a debugger? There are lots of tools that are “debugging tools” but when most people hear “debugger” they usually think of a tool that can analyze either a running system or a static snapshot (such as a core file, crash dump, or VM snapshot)1. Most debuggers like GDB, LLDB, Visual Studio, and WinDbg can do both of these things. We’ll start by creating a debugger that supports live usermode debugging on Windows. The core concepts will apply to nearly any OS, with the main differences being the OS APIs for debugging a process and the terminology that is used for certain concepts.

blocks.html_en: In Windows, there are just a few APIs that provide the necessary functionality for implementing a debugger. Most of these are described on MSDN in the Debugging Functions page. The core engine of WinDbg is called DbgEng, and has its own set of APIs that can be accessed through the IDebugClient interface and related APIs. These higher level APIs and are very powerful, with built in stack unwinding, symbol analysis, flow control, disassembly, scripting, and lots of other capabilities. blocks.html_en: At the center of a live debugging session is an event loop. A debugger registers for debug events from a target process by “attaching” to it. For each event that occurs, the OS will freeze the target process and notify the debugger with information about that debug event. The debugger then has the opportunity to examine or manipulate the state of the target process. The debugger then continues from the debug event.

我已经两次离开 Microsoft 调试器平台团队，每次我都开始编写自己的调试器。 我一定很喜欢调试器之类的东西。 这次，我编写新的调试器有两个原因。 首先是因为我想更好地学习 Rust，而写一些我已经很理解的东西似乎是一种很好的学习方式。 第二个原因是为了让人们更容易了解调试器的工作原理。 使用 Rust 在这里也有帮助，因为有很多包可以处理符号和反汇编等事情，它会让我们专注于编写调试器所涉及的核心思想。

我是 Rust 新手，如果你想更好地学习 Rust，我建议从 https://www.rust-lang.org/learn 开始。我不会尝试过多解释 Rust 代码，但主要概念和 API 将适用于各种语言。 即使您对 Rust 没有太多了解，也应该能够跟上。 那些读过本文并且比我更了解 Rust 的人，请随时在 GitHub 存储库中创建问题。 或者更好的是，提出拉取请求！ 第一部分的代码位于名为“part1”的分支中，您可以在此处查看完整的代码。 如果您想继续操作，我建议在本地克隆整个存储库，并使用 rust-analyzer 插件在 VS Code 等优秀 IDE 中查看它。

什么是调试器？

首先，什么是调试器？ 有很多工具都是“调试工具”，但是当大多数人听到“调试器”时，他们通常会想到可以分析正在运行的系统或静态快照（例如核心文件、故障转储或虚拟机快照）的工具1。 大多数调试器（例如 GDB、LLDB、Visual Studio 和 WinDbg）都可以完成这两件事。 我们将首先创建一个支持 Windows 上实时用户模式调试的调试器。 核心概念几乎适用于任何操作系统，主要区别在于用于调试进程的操作系统 API 以及用于某些概念的术语。

在 Windows 中，只有少数 API 提供了实现调试器所需的功能。 其中大部分在 MSDN 的“调试功能”页面中进行了描述。 请注意，这些是由 Visual Studio 或 WinDbg 等调试器使用的 API。 WinDbg的核心引擎称为DbgEng，有自己的一套API，可以通过IDebugClient接口和相关API来访问。 这些更高级别的 API 非常强大，具有内置的堆栈展开、符号分析、流程控制、反汇编、脚本编写和许多其他功能。 如果您想自动执行某些调试任务，这是一个更好的 API。 但这不是我们在本系列文章中要做的事情。 我们将使用操作系统提供的最基本的 API 从头开始​​实现一个调试器。

我们还需要许多其他函数来与正在运行的进程交互，但这些 API 不是特定于调试的。 当我们遇到这些问题时，我们会进行介绍。

基本结构

实时调试会话的中心是事件循环。 调试器通过“附加”到目标进程来注册调试事件。 对于发生的每个事件，操作系统将冻结目标进程并通知调试器有关该调试事件的信息。 然后，调试器有机会检查或操作目标进程的状态。 然后调试器从调试事件继续。

这里嵌入了大量的复杂性，但大部分复杂性在于检查和操作目标进程的状态。 我们将首先创建一个附加到进程的调试器，监视调试事件，并从它们继续以允许进程正常执行。 该部分相对简单，将为我们在此基础上构建其他功能奠定基础。

在 Windows 上，有两种主要方法可以附加到进程。 如果我们想要附加到的进程已经在运行，我们可以使用 DebugActiveProcess API，它采用带有我们想要调试的进程 ID 的单个参数。2。 此 API 调用不会返回任何句柄或任何其他信息。 相反，在目标进程和调试器进程之间创建隐式连接。 要停止调试进程，请调用 DebugActiveProcessStop，它也采用进程 ID 的单个参数。

附加到进程的第二种方法是创建处于附加状态的进程。 为此，我们使用通常用于调试进程的相同 CreateProcessW 函数，并将 DEBUG_ONLY_THIS_PROCESS 或 DEBUG_PROCESS 标志作为 dwCreationFlags 参数的一部分（记录为进程创建标志的一部分）。 这些标志之间的区别在于您是否只想调试启动的特定进程，或者是否想要调试该进程及其所有子进程。

我们将使用 CreateProcessW 开始调试进程：

CreateProcessW有很多参数，但是我们可以忽略可选参数来启动。 稍后，我们可能希望为该调试器的用户提供自定义某些方面的能力，但现在我们将简单地使用作为 lpCommandLine 传入的整个命令行。 如果您想了解我们如何启动命令行，请参阅该项目的 github 存储库中的 parse_command_line 。 我们还将传递 DEBUG_ONLY_THIS_PROCESS 标志作为 dwCreationFlags 的一部分。 我还指定了 CREATE_NEW_CONSOLE，这样我们在调试控制台应用程序时就不会共享控制台（CDB/NTSD 将与目标共享控制台，我总是发现这很令人困惑，而且很少有用）。 最后，我们将收到一些重要信息作为 lpProcessInformation 参数的一部分，该参数是一个输出参数。

当CreateProcessW返回时，该进程将首先被挂起。 在调试器进程开始处理调试事件之前，不会执行任何代码。 这就是我们接下来要做的。

监控调试事件

有两个函数用于驱动 Windows 中调试器的事件循环。 第一个是 WaitForDebugEventEx 函数3。 第二个函数是ContinueDebugEvent，它将在处理事件后恢复目标进程。 我们将从 main_debugger_loop 调用这些函数。

56    loop {
57        let mut debug_event: DEBUG_EVENT = unsafe { std::mem::zeroed() };
58        unsafe {
59            WaitForDebugEventEx(&mut debug_event, INFINITE);
60        }

main.rs 第 56 行

您可能会注意到这里有趣的是 WaitForDebugEventEx 函数不接受任何进程标识符。 如果一个进程附加到多个目标进程，则对 WaitForDebugEventEx 的任何调用都将监视所有附加进程的事件4。 INFINITE 参数意味着我们将永远等待，直到收到调试事件。 该事件被描述为 DEBUG_EVENT 结构，其中包含线程 ID、进程 ID 和事件代码字段。 每个事件类型都有自己的数据结构，并且这些结构作为联合存储。 您可以使用事件代码来确定联合中的哪个结构有效。

typedef struct _DEBUG_EVENT {
  DWORD dwDebugEventCode;
  DWORD dwProcessId;
  DWORD dwThreadId;
  union {
    EXCEPTION_DEBUG_INFO      Exception;
    CREATE_THREAD_DEBUG_INFO  CreateThread;
    CREATE_PROCESS_DEBUG_INFO CreateProcessInfo;
    EXIT_THREAD_DEBUG_INFO    ExitThread;
    EXIT_PROCESS_DEBUG_INFO   ExitProcess;
    LOAD_DLL_DEBUG_INFO       LoadDll;
    UNLOAD_DLL_DEBUG_INFO     UnloadDll;
    OUTPUT_DEBUG_STRING_INFO  DebugString;
    RIP_INFO                  RipInfo;
  } u;
} DEBUG_EVENT, *LPDEBUG_EVENT;

我们将在后面的文章中深入研究这些数据。 现在，我们可以只输出我们收到的事件。

这些行中的每一行都代表从 WaitForDebugEventEx 返回的单个事件。 这些事件中的每一个也是调试器检查进程状态的机会。 我们还没有开始查看每个事件的具体信息（例如加载的 DLL 的名称），但是您可以看到 WinDbg 如何实现像 sxe ld 这样的命令，其中调试器可以在模块加载后立即“中断”。 实时调试进程时“闯入”的全部含义就是在调用ContinueDebugEvent 之前等待。 返回这些事件之一后，我们可以允许交互式用户运行一些命令来检查进程的状态。 当它们完成并执行像 g 这样的命令继续执行时，调试器将调用ContinueDebugEvent，然后再次调用WaitForDebugEventEx以等待下一个事件。

大多数这些事件看起来都很合理。 我们期望加载一堆 DLL，创建一些线程，最终卸载一些 DLL 并退出线程和进程。 中间隐藏着一个事件，它是一个异常。 这是 ntdll!LdrpDoDebuggerBreak! 的初始断点！ 作为进程启动的一部分，ntdll 将在 x865 上使用显式 int 3 触发断点异常。

我们如何处理异常事件将是调试实时进程的最重要部分之一。 从断点、单步执行到应用程序崩溃的所有事情都通过异常事件进行管理。 我们需要花一些时间来确保正确处理这个问题，所以我将把它留到下一篇文章中。 在那之前，请在 Twitter 或 Mastodon 上告诉我您对此有何看法！

脚注

1 许多调试器还与某种形式的“时间旅行调试”集成，其中以不同粒度级别捕获执行跟踪。 虽然我们在这里讨论的许多概念也适用于时间旅行调试，但为了简洁起见，我将在这里跳过讨论。

2 使用此 API 将检查调用进程是否确实具有足够的权限来附加到所请求的进程。 您通常无法附加到提升的进程或从未提升的进程中为其他用户运行的进程。 还有某些进程即使是提升的管理员进程也无法直接附加到。 文档将其描述为“它必须能够打开 PROCESS_ALL_ACCESS 的进程。

3 有一个WaitForDebugEvent 函数（不带“Ex”），但该函数无法正确接收从OutputDebugStringW 生成的Unicode 字符串。 我们需要 Unicode 字符串，因此我们将使用“Ex”版本。

4 这意味着两个单独的模块不可能从单个进程调试两个单独的目标。 这些是非常古老的 API，依赖于进程范围的状态，并且永远不能被期望加载到任意进程的模块使用。 幸运的是，这在实践中很少出现问题。

5 仅当进程正在调试时才会触发该断点。 这是通过检查 PEB 的“BeingDebugged”标志来检测的。 如果您在初始断点之前中断进程并将该标志设置为“0”，则将跳过初始断点。
